meta.title: Khetwadicha Ganraj - 12th Lane
meta.location: 12th Khetwadi Lane, Girgaon / Grant Road, Mumbai
meta.foundedNote: The exact 12th-lane institution dates its foundation to 1959 in its legacy history. A newer same-name site gives 1952, but its connection to this institution has not been established.
meta.intro: Khetwadicha Ganraj is the 12th Khetwadi Sarvajanik Ganeshotsav Mandal, one institution among separate lane festivals. Its legacy history recalls small subscriptions, a tall-idol initiative in 1984 and a 40-foot Parashuram form in 2000. The expanded image record distinguishes treated historical cards from photographs of physical throne and palace displays in 2009-2025. The institution's 1959 foundation account is retained, while conflicting anniversary counts and an unlinked same-name 1952 claim remain qualified.

sections.title: A lane is part of the name

paragraphs.text: The legacy institutional website explicitly identifies 12th Khetwadi and dates the mandal to 1959; its contact page locates the organization in 12th Khetwadi Lane. A newer same-name website claims 1952, but no institutional linkage has been established. That claim remains an unverified source lead rather than a competing foundation date for this exact mandal.

The older account describes one-rupee donations, an initiative toward tall idols from 1984 and a 40-foot Parashuram composition in 2000, followed by a golden-jubilee celebration in 2008. These are useful institutional milestones. Its India-wide tallest claim lacks an inspected contemporary comparative record or common measurement convention, so the archive presents the remembered height without certifying a universal record.

sections.title: What the 2022 eyewitness report actually says

paragraphs.text: A detailed Indian Express visit in 2022 locates Vinayaki in the 8th lane, Parashuram in the 11th, an airborne Rama form in Khambata Lane and a fictional Rajasthani Radha-Krishna palace in the 12th. Some broad roundups and later summaries collapse those identities. The specific street-by-street account and its matched photographs are preferred for annual attribution.

sections.title: A neighborhood reached through new media

paragraphs.text: Times of India reported the 12th-lane mandal’s mobile app in 2014, explaining online viewing for those unable to visit crowded lanes. Marathi reporting in 2026 again distinguishes the 12th-lane throne-and-Hanuman presentation from 7th- and 11th-lane themes. These records support continuity of public presentation without assigning one fixed form to every year.

The expanded selection contains physical display photographs from 2009-2012,2014-2019,2022 and 2025, alongside three separately marked treated historical cards. Exact-lane captions and year evidence govern annual attribution. Visual resemblance, upload folders and costumes are insufficient to move a frame across lanes or years.

sections.title: Historical cards and physical displays are different evidence

paragraphs.text: The legacy gallery supplies explicit annual labels, but most early objects are modern devotional cards: an old idol cutout placed over new scenery, with printed year and height. The 1983 tortoise form is labelled 30 feet; the 1984 fish form 28 feet; the 2000 Parashuram form 40 feet. Their digital treatment and attribution remain visible in the archive. They cannot establish original camera dates or independently verify the dimensions.

This exposes an internal inconsistency. The same institution's narrative begins its tall-idol initiative in 1984, while its 1983 card already reports 30 feet. An original souvenir, contemporary report or dated print is needed to decide whether the narrative refers to a particular initiative, whether a card is misdated, or whether another explanation applies. None is assumed.

The 2009-2011 gallery items retain physical throne and pandal settings. Later photographs identify exact 12th Lane through individual captions, credited authors or uploader descriptions. Different clothing in pictures can reflect changes within one festival, so costume alone is not used to invent extra annual records. A 2012 blog's 21-headed martial caption and several online 11th/12th Lane mix-ups are excluded from the selected series.

Contemporary 2011 reporting describes a lamp-palace setting with 10001 artificial diyas and young gana sevak volunteers. In 2012, a mandal representative described 35-40 artisans preparing a setting inspired by Babulnath's ISKCON temple. These dated accounts connect the large public display to volunteer participation and the labor of temporary architecture; they are not evidence that the same set or workforce repeated unchanged.

A 2015 photographer explicitly credits Raju Shinde for Ganraj. This provides one source-attributed annual artist credit, rather than proving an uninterrupted appointment across every year in the archive. The 2025 palace photograph and its contemporary reports show a later architectural conception, while incompatible press anniversary counts are retained as a source discrepancy.
